request.system:
You are the reasoning step of an enterprise agent working on behalf of one named employee. You do not act. You propose, and a human decides.

Your job: given something a detector noticed and the context that could be gathered about it, recommend the single best response.

Rules you must follow:

1. Prefer a declared workflow when one fits. Workflows encode how this company has    decided the work must be done; entering one means the steps run in their declared    order whether or not you agree with the order. Supply its parameters accurately    and do not describe the steps as though you were choosing them.
2. Use individual tool calls only when no declared workflow covers the situation.    When you do, propose the *complete* response, not just its first step. If your    action changes what another team will find when they next look — a different lot    on the line, a different supplier on the dock, a date that moved — then telling    the person responsible is part of the response, not an optional extra. A half    plan is worse than none, because the human approves it believing it is whole.
3. Order tool calls so that anything irreversible comes last. A message cannot be    unsent, so send it once the changes it describes have actually been made. If an    earlier step fails, the ones before it can be undone and nobody has been told    something untrue.
4. If nothing is warranted, say so with action_kind "none" and explain why. A false    alarm dismissed with a reason is a good outcome.
5. Cite the specific records that led you to your conclusion. Refer to them by their    identifiers, exactly as they appear in the context.
6. Some systems may have been unreadable for this user. If something you would want    to check was not available, say so in your reasoning rather than assuming what it    would have contained.
7. Beliefs listed under "remembered_beliefs" are advisory background from earlier    runs, not current facts. They may inform how you weigh options. Never treat one    as evidence of the present state of a system.

Your summary will be shown to a busy manager as the first and possibly only thing they read. One sentence: what is wrong, and what you propose to do.

evidence.detail: P-4471 shortfall will delay production order 4812; projected on-hand is 0 at start of production
Production order 4812 scheduled to start 2026-09-07, needs 120 units of P-4471
150 on hand with 30/day usage; 5 days of cover means zero at 2026-09-07
PO-77812 revised delivery from 2026-09-04 to 2026-09-08, one day after production start
Meridian Drives approved for P-4471, 2-day lead time, $46.5/unit, 0.94 on-time rate

output.reasoning:
The detector has identified a genuine shortage: production order 4812 requires 120 units of P-4471 (stepper motor) and is scheduled to start 2026-09-07. The current stock of 150 units will be consumed at 30/day, leaving zero on hand by the start date (baseline_consumption_before_start: 150). The only incoming purchase order PO-77812 arrives 2026-09-08, one day late per email M-001 from Kestrel Components (S-Y) dated 2026-09-01 (revised_by_supplier: true).

The company has a declared workflow "po_reroute" (version 3) specifically designed for this scenario: replacing an at-risk PO with a faster supplier. I examined the approved suppliers for P-4471 from the ERP context:

- S-Q (Apex Rapid Supply): Not approved for P-4471 (only P-9002)
- S-T (Voss Antriebe): Not approved for P-4471 (only P-5540)
- S-V (Northwind): Not approved for P-4471 (only P-1188)
- S-W (Halstead Precision): Approved for P-4471, 9-day lead time, too slow
- S-Y (Kestrel Components): Current supplier, 6-day lead time, already failed
- S-Z (Meridian Drives): Approved for P-4471, 2-day lead time at $46.5/unit, 0.94 on-time rate

If an order is placed today (2026-09-02) with S-Z, delivery in 2 days arrives 2026-09-04, well before the 2026-09-07 production start. S-Z has the best on-time performance (0.94) among available options and can deliver the full 120 units needed (or more, to ensure coverage).

The workflow will handle supplier selection, PO creation, cancellation of the old order, notification to production supervisor u-301, and arrival verification—all in the correct sequence with messaging only after changes are committed. This follows rule 1 (prefer declared workflows) and rule 3 (irreversible actions last).

Evidence: detector findings (P-4471, production_order 4812), ERP supplier records showing S-Z's capabilities, and mail M-001 confirming S-Y's revised delivery date after the production start.
output.summary: Production order 4812 will be short 120 units of P-4471 on its 2026-09-07 start because the current PO-77812 arrives 2026-09-08; propose rerouting to Meridian Drives (S-Z) with 2-day lead time to arrive in time.
